newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire, rebels set conditions for rescue force.
newsitem.headline: Zaire, rebels set conditions for rescue force.

text.p: The Zairean government and rebels in the far east of the country between them rejected on Saturday most of the ideas for a multinational military force set up to help refugees in eastern Zaire.

After talks in Kinshasa with the Canadian commander of the force, Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, Interior Minister Kamanda Wa Kamanda said that his government opposed one of the two main options, airdropping supplies into rebel-held areas.
At a news conference in the rebel-held town of Goma earlier, rebel leader Laurent Kabila said any military intervention by the force would have to be very limited.
The rebels are especially hostile towards the second option, sending in troops to escort aid convoys, on the grounds that this could strengthen the hand of the Zairean army.

Kabila, who met Baril in Goma on Thursday, said: "We (Baril and I) agreed that they can only send a small group of soldiers, not more than five, who would be specialists. Their duties would be to coordinate airdrops."
"But they cannot drop food, because it will feed the enemy," he said, sitting on a pink and gold striped sofa in what used to be the palace of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"We will allow them to drop food if we are informed of a big concentration of refugees, but it is a stupid idea," he added.

In Kinshasa, Kamanda said: "We do not understand how the multinational force could operate in Zaire without taking into account...the fact that we are at war with the regular armies of Rwanda and Burundi, supported by Uganda."
"We remain formally against the airdropping of supplies," the interior minister added.
Baril said he was travelling on to Uganda later on Saturday. From there he would let his superiors know the position of the Zairean government and try to incorporate it into plans.

"Our mission is strictly humanitarian and has absolutely no political or military angles. We will not involve ourselves in disputes on the ground and will not coordinate with whoever controls the territory," he said.
Ambassadors from 14 countries gave the green light for the Canadian-led force at a meeting in Ottawa on Friday.

More than 20 countries including the United States, France, Britain, Belgium, Senegal and South Africa will contribute to the mission, more likely to comprise 1,000 or 2,000 troops than the 10,000 originally planned.

The aim is to find and rescue up to 600,000 people adrift in the area, mostly Rwandan refugees and displaced Zaireans. They include some of the Rwandan Hutu militiamen responsible for massacring up to one million people in Rwanda in 1994.
The rebels, known as the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, moved on Saturday deeper into southeastern Zaire from Bukavu on the Rwandan border.
They said their target was the Kamituga area, where they expect Zairean troops to make a stand to protect the rich gold and diamond diggings nearby.
A convoy of trucks, buses, cars and motorbikes packed with heavily armed rebel troops was on the move near Chimanga, about 100 km (60 miles) southwest of Bukavu.

Rebel troops patrolling in the area said remnants of the Zairean army they crushed last month were regrouping with former Rwandan army soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen from the abandoned Hutu refugee camp at Chimanga.
"The area is not safe," said one soldier. "There has been a lot of fighting."

In Bukavu, trucks packed with new recruits to the rebel force roared through the streets on Saturday evening. The recruits, mainly ethnic Tutsis -- an important element in the rebel force -- were cheering and singing victory songs.
Another force, the Ugandan army, has now joined the fray in Central Africa, the Ugandan government paper New Vision said.
Close to the northern limit of the rebel zone, the Ugandan army crossed the border into Zaire on Thursday and seized the town of Kasindi and parts of the Virunga hills, it said.

It quoted local Ugandan army commander Lieutenant-Colonel Geoffrey Muheesi as saying it was an operation against Ugandan rebels who have been attacking from Zaire. "We are fed up with these bandits. We are going to finish them," he said.
